claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with uniformly distributed constituent elements.
High mechanical loading causes stress-induced atomic segregation in the alloy.
Stress-induced segregation causes brittle intermetallic precipitates to nucleate and grow.
The brittle intermetallic precipitates act as local fracture-initiation sites.
Formation of the precipitates causes a loss of toughness and a shift toward brittle fracture.
Brittle intermetallic precipitates preferentially form at stress concentrators such as grain boundaries and dislocation intersections.
Applied mechanical stress accelerates local atomic mobility and segregation.
Moderate-to-high temperature increases the likelihood of diffusion and local segregation during loading.
Brittle phases embedded in the otherwise ductile matrix act as microstructural weak points.
High-cycle-fatigue-loaded specimens will have lower fracture toughness than unloaded or lower-load controls.
Brittle intermetallic precipitates will be detectable in highly loaded specimens and absent from control specimens.
Unstrained or lower-stress baseline specimens retain a stable single-phase solid solution and high toughness.
The proposed embrittlement occurs only when stress amplitude and temperature are sufficient to enable significant atomic mobility.
Below the relevant stress and temperature thresholds, the alloy retains its toughness.
The temperature and loading-amplitude thresholds for segregation and precipitation are undetermined.
Cyclic-loading-induced dislocation structures may also contribute to the observed behavior.
